title: Sudden paraplegia after a fleeting chest pain

source.citation: Nagarajan S, Ganessane E, Kowsthubha BG, Somasundaram A, Balamurugan N. A Diagnostic Pitfall in the Emergency Department -Aortic Dissection Masquerading as Acute Paraplegia: A Case Report. Clin Pract Cases Emerg Med. 2026;10(3):380-384.

presentation.chiefComplaint: Sudden inability to move both legs
presentation.hpi: Well until this morning, when he had a few minutes of central, non-radiating chest pain with sweating and palpitations that settled by itself; no dyspnea or syncope. Soon afterwards both legs began to tingle and go numb, progressing rapidly to complete paralysis with urinary incontinence. A nearby hospital obtained a lumbar spine CT 3–4 h after onset, which was unremarkable. With no diagnosis, he was transferred and arrives about 17 h after symptom onset.
pmh: No known hypertension, diabetes mellitus or connective tissue disease
presentation.social: Lives with his wife and is independent in daily activities. Never smoked; drinks alcohol rarely; denies cocaine or other drug use.

exam: Alert and oriented; general physical examination otherwise unremarkable
Normal heart sounds without murmurs; respiratory and abdominal examinations normal
Flaccid paralysis of both legs: power 0/5, absent deep tendon reflexes, mute plantar responses
Loss of pain and temperature sensation below L1 with preserved vibration and proprioception
Cranial nerves and upper limbs normal
Peripheral pulses palpable and symmetric in all four limbs
Four-limb blood pressure (checked later): right arm 170/110, left arm 182/100, both legs 180/100 mm Hg
About 6 h after arrival, while under observation: new, worsening tachypnea

investigations.name: Arterial blood gas (6 h after arrival)
investigations.value: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with raised lactate

imaging.finding: Stanford type A dissection of the ascending aorta and arch with aneurysmal dilatation, extending into the descending thoracic aorta. Celiac, superior mesenteric and right renal arteries arise from the true lumen; the left renal artery arises from the false lumen (non-opacified left kidney). False lumen partly thrombosed; no active hemorrhage.

ecg: Sinus rhythm 76/min, normal axis, no acute ST-segment or T-wave changes

diagnosis.primary: Acute Stanford type A aortic dissection with spinal cord ischemia (anterior spinal artery syndrome) and left renal malperfusion
differentials: Anterior spinal artery infarction from another cause

management: Urgent surgical repair recommended; the patient declined surgery and chose supportive medical care
Intravenous labetalol infusion for blood pressure control
Hemodialysis (several sessions) for progressive renal failure
outcome: Progressive renal failure from left renal artery ischemia with worsening metabolic acidosis; died of uremic complications 5 days after admission.
teachingPoints: Aortic dissection can present with neurological deficits and little or no pain; consider it in any acute non-traumatic paraplegia.
Anterior spinal artery syndrome: paraplegia, areflexia and loss of pain and temperature sensation with preserved vibration and proprioception.
Symmetric pulses and limb pressures do not exclude dissection (pulse deficits are present in only a minority).
New lactic acidosis or rising creatinine in a 'neurological' patient suggests malperfusion; image the whole aorta.
Type A dissection needs emergency surgery; meanwhile beta-blockade first, then vasodilators, to cut aortic wall stress.

questions.q: What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.extra: 6 h after arrival: new tachypnea. ABG pH 7.24, HCO3⁻ 11 mmol/L, anion gap 24, lactate 7.2 mmol/L. Chest radiograph: widened mediastinum.
options: CT angiography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis
questions.explanation: Paraplegia that followed chest pain, plus new lactic acidosis and a widened mediastinum, makes an acute aortic syndrome likely; in a stable patient CT angiography of the whole aorta is the first-line test (ESC 2014 aortic disease guidelines; 2022 ACC/AHA aortic disease guideline). Spine MRI would delay the diagnosis that matters.

questions.q: The neurological findings are best explained by ischemia in which territory?
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery feeds the anterior two-thirds of the cord (corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts) and spares the dorsal columns, hence lost power and pain/temperature with preserved vibration and proprioception. Dissection can cut off the artery of Adamkiewicz, which usually arises from the aorta between T9 and L2.

questions.q: While cardiothoracic surgery is called, which blood pressure strategy is most appropriate?
questions.extra: CT angiography: Stanford type A dissection from the ascending aorta to the descending thoracic aorta; left renal artery from the false lumen. BP 182/100 mm Hg, HR 80/min.
options: IV nitroprusside alone, titrated quickly to an SBP below 120 mm Hg
IV hydralazine boluses every 20 minutes until SBP is below 140 mm Hg
IV esmolol or labetalol first, adding a vasodilator if SBP stays above 120 mm Hg
Oral amlodipine, with a repeat blood pressure in one hour
questions.explanation: Anti-impulse therapy starts with an IV beta-blocker to lower heart rate and aortic wall shear stress; a vasodilator given alone causes reflex tachycardia. Usual targets are a heart rate around 60/min and SBP 100–120 mm Hg (ESC 2014 aortic disease guidelines; 2022 ACC/AHA aortic disease guideline).

questions.q: What is the definitive treatment of choice?
questions.extra: CT angiography: Stanford type A dissection from the ascending aorta to the descending thoracic aorta; left renal artery from the false lumen.
options: Thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) of the descending aorta
Medical therapy alone, since the false lumen is partly thrombosed
Delayed elective repair once renal function has recovered
Emergency open surgical repair of the ascending aorta and arch
questions.explanation: Type A dissection is a surgical emergency (ESC 2014; 2022 ACC/AHA): untreated mortality rises by roughly 1–2% per hour early on and approaches 50% at 48 h. TEVAR is mainly for complicated type B dissection, and malperfusion is a reason for urgency, not delay.

evidence.quote: We report a 52-year-old male who presented with sudden-onset paraplegia.
he developed an episode of central, nonradiating chest pain associated with diaphoresis and palpitations. The pain lasted for a few minutes and resolved spontaneously
he developed tingling and numbness in both lower limbs, which rapidly progressed to complete paralysis, accompanied by urinary incontinence
computed tomography of the lumbar spine was performed to evaluate for spinal pathology and showed no acute abnormality
he was referred to our tertiary care center, where he arrived approximately 17 hours after symptom onset
His medical history was notable only for congenital blindness.
There was no known history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or connective tissue disease.
heart rate, 76 beats per minute; respiratory rate, 20 breaths per minute; blood pressure, 170/110 mm Hg
temperature; 37 °C; and oxygen saturation, 98% on room air
the patient was alert and oriented … The general physical examination was unremarkable.
Cardiovascular examination demonstrated normal heart sounds without murmurs. Respiratory and abdominal examinations were normal.
paralysis of both lower limbs with motor strength 0/5, absent deep tendon reflexes, and mute plantar responses
loss of pain and temperature sensation below the first lumbar dermatome with preserved vibration and proprioception, consistent with anterior spinal artery syndrome
Cranial nerve and upper limb examinations were normal.
Peripheral pulses were palpable and symmetric in all four extremities.
170/110 mm Hg in the right upper limb, 182/100 mm Hg in the left upper limb, and 180/100 mm Hg in both lower limbs
Approximately six hours after arrival, while he was under observation in the ED, he developed worsening tachypnea
The arterial blood gas analysis revealed a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate levels
hemoglobin,12.9 g/dL (reference range, 13.1–17.2 g/dL); urea, 40 mg/dL (17–43 mg/dL); and creatinine, 1.9 mg/dL (0.6–1.17 mg/dL)
A chest radiograph demonstrated a widened mediastinum
a Stanford type A aortic dissection involving the ascending aorta and aortic arch, associated with aneurysmal dilatation, with extension into the descending thoracic aorta
The right renal artery originated from the true lumen, while the left renal artery arose from the false lumen.
Partial thrombosis of the false lumen was noted, without evidence of active hemorrhage
counseled regarding the need for urgent surgical repair, but he declined operative intervention and opted for supportive medical management
Blood pressure was controlled with an intravenous labetalol infusion.
the patient developed progressive renal failure secondary to left renal artery ischemia and worsening metabolic acidosis
He underwent multiple sessions of hemodialysis but continued to deteriorate and subsequently succumbed five days after admission due to uremic complications.
